lessons.title: Nutritional Needs of Honey Bees
lessons.body: Honey bees need carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, minerals, and water. Carbohydrates come from nectar and honey, providing energy for flight and colony activities. A strong colony consumes 20â30 kg of honey per year. Proteins come from pollen, essential for brood rearing and gland development. A colony collects 20â30 kg of pollen annually. Lipids, vitamins, and minerals are also in pollen. Without enough pollen, nurse bees cannot produce royal jelly, and brood rearing stops. In Africa, dearth periods (dry seasons) can last 3â6 months, so beekeepers must monitor stores. A colony needs at least 5â10 kg of honey stored to survive a dearth. If honey stores are low, feed sugar syrup. Pollen shortages cause stunted brood and reduced lifespan. You can check pollen stores by inspecting frames: look for cells packed with pollen (bee bread) in various colors. If less than one full frame of pollen, feed pollen patties. Water is critical for cooling and diluting honey; a colony uses 1â2 liters per day in hot weather. Place water sources within 500 meters. In summary, bees need sugar for energy, pollen for growth, and water for survival. Regular inspections and supplemental feeding during dearth keep colonies strong.

lessons.title: Natural Forage and Pollen Sources
lessons.body: Natural forage includes nectar and pollen from flowering plants. In Africa, key bee plants vary by region. Acacia species (e.g., Acacia tortilis) provide nectar and pollen in dry areas. Sunflower, canola, and cotton are major crops. Indigenous trees like Croton, Combretum, and Protea are excellent. Aloe species flower in winter, providing critical forage when little else blooms. Fruit trees (mango, citrus, avocado) offer early nectar. Herbs like basil, rosemary, and thyme attract bees. Weeds like dandelion and clover are valuable. A diverse landscape ensures continuous bloom. Bees forage up to 3 km from the hive, but most foraging occurs within 1 km. To assess forage, observe bee activity: if bees return with pollen loads (colored balls on legs), forage is good. During dearth, bees may rob other hives or starve. Plant or conserve bee-friendly species. In East Africa, the flowering calendar: MarchâMay (long rains) â many wildflowers; JuneâAugust (dry) â acacia, aloe; SeptemberâNovember (short rains) â crops; DecemberâFebruary (dry) â irrigation crops. Beekeepers can plant fast-growing species like sunflower, which flowers in 60â90 days. Avoid monocultures; mix trees, shrubs, and herbs. Protect existing forage from burning and clearing. A good forage plan reduces feeding costs and boosts honey yields.

lessons.title: Supplemental Feeding: Sugar Syrup and Pollen Patties
lessons.body: Supplemental feeding is needed when natural forage is scarce, during dearth or after swarming. Sugar syrup: mix 1 kg white sugar with 1 liter clean water (1:1) for spring stimulation; use 2:1 (2 kg sugar to 1 liter water) for autumn stores. Never use brown sugar, honey from unknown sources, or artificial sweetenersâthey can cause dysentery or disease. Heat water, add sugar, stir until dissolved, cool. Feed inside the hive using a feeder (frame feeder, top feeder, or plastic bag with small holes). For 1:1, feed 500 ml per colony every 3 days. For 2:1, feed 1 liter per week. Stop when bees stop taking it or when natural forage returns. Pollen patties: mix 1 part soy flour, 1 part brewerâs yeast, 1 part sugar, and enough sugar syrup to make a stiff dough. Add 1 teaspoon of vitamin C per kg. Shape into patties (200â300 g) and place on top bars, covered with wax paper. Feed every 7â10 days until pollen comes in. In Africa, alternatives: use local pollen from healthy hives (freeze for 48 hours to kill pests), or mix dried cowpea flour. Always feed at dusk to prevent robbing. Clean feeders to avoid mold. Record feeding dates and amounts.

lessons.title: Planting for Bees: Bee-Friendly Gardens
lessons.body: Planting bee-friendly gardens ensures year-round forage. Choose plants with different flowering times. In Africa, good choices: Sunflower (Helianthus annuus) â flowers in 60â90 days, high nectar and pollen. Lavender (Lavandula spp.) â drought-tolerant, flowers in dry season. Basil (Ocimum spp.) â fast-growing, bees love it. Marigold (Tagetes spp.) â pest repellent and bee forage. Aloe (Aloe spp.) â winter flowers. Acacia (Acacia spp.) â long-lived, dry-season nectar. Fruit trees: mango, citrus, avocado. Plant in clusters of 1â2 meters apart. Prepare soil with compost. Water young plants until established. Avoid pesticides. For a small garden (10x10 m), plant 10 sunflowers, 5 lavender, 5 basil, and 2 fruit trees. This can support 1â2 hives. For larger apiaries, plant hedgerows of bee plants along boundaries. In dry areas, use drip irrigation. Mulch to retain moisture. Rotate crops to avoid pests. Bees need continuous bloom: aim for at least 3 species flowering each month. In East Africa, plant fast-growing species like sunflower and basil for quick results. Indigenous trees like Croton and Combretum take longer but provide long-term forage. Involve the community; avoid burning grasslands. A well-planted garden reduces feeding costs and increases honey production by 20â30%.

lessons.title: Water Sources for Bees
lessons.body: Bees need water for cooling the hive, diluting honey, and rearing brood. A colony uses 1â2 liters per day in hot weather. Without water, bees may die or abandon the hive. Provide a reliable water source within 500 meters. Options: shallow trays with stones or floating sticks so bees can land and drink without drowning. Refill daily. A dripping tap or slow-drip irrigation line works. Place water in partial shade to reduce evaporation. Add a pinch of salt (1 teaspoon per 4 liters) to provide minerals; bees prefer slightly salty water. Avoid chlorinated water; let it sit for 24 hours. In dry regions, create a small pond with clay lining. Keep water clean; change every 2â3 days to prevent mosquito breeding. If natural water is far, set up a drum with a tap and a trough. In African villages, communal water points can be used, but ensure bees have safe access. Never place water inside the hiveâit increases humidity and mold. In hot climates, provide water near the hive entrance. Monitor water consumption: if bees ignore it, they may have a natural source. During dearth, water is critical. A simple solution: a 20-liter bucket with a small hole dripping into a tray with stones. This costs little and saves colonies. Always check water sources during inspections.

lessons.title: Avoiding Pesticide Poisoning
lessons.body: Pesticides kill bees. Common signs: dead bees at hive entrance, disoriented bees, sudden brood loss, queen death. In Africa, farmers often use insecticides like cypermethrin, dimethoate, and chlorpyrifos. To avoid poisoning: 1) Talk to neighbouring farmers. Ask them to spray at dusk when bees are not flying. 2) Use bee-safe pesticides: neem oil, Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt), soap sprays. 3) Never spray on flowering crops. 4) If spraying is necessary, cover hives with wet burlap and provide shade. 5) Keep hives away from sprayed fields by at least 3 km. 6) Report pesticide kills to local authorities. 7) Plant border crops like sunflower to lure bees away. 8) Use integrated pest management (IPM): handpick pests, use traps, encourage natural enemies. 9) If you must spray, use a knapsack sprayer with a fine nozzle, not foggers. 10) Always read labels; many pesticides are highly toxic to bees. In case of poisoning: remove dead bees, feed sugar syrup, add a new queen if needed. Prevent future exposure. Educate your community. In Kenya, the Pest Control Products Board regulates pesticides. Beekeepers can advocate for bee-friendly practices. Remember: one spray can kill 20,000 bees. Protect your hives by communicating with farmers and using organic methods.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Bee Nutrition and Forage Management for African Apiaries

This practical reference consolidates the six lessons of the Bee Nutrition and Forage module into a single field-ready guide for African beekeepers, extension officers, and agribusiness operators. It is written business-first: every recommendation is framed around colony productivity, honey yield, pollination income, and cost control. Whether you manage ten hives in a homestead or two hundred hives for commercial honey and pollination contracts, the principles here determine your margins. A colony that is malnourished produces less honey, swarms more often, absconds more readily, and is more vulnerable to pests and disease â all of which directly reduce revenue.

1. Nutritional Needs of Honey Bees

Honey bees require four broad nutritional categories: carbohydrates (energy, mainly from nectar and honey), proteins and amino acids (from pollen, essential for brood rearing and gland development), lipids and sterols (from pollen, needed for cell membranes and hormone synthesis), and minerals and vitamins (from pollen, nectar, and water). The balance matters more than any single nutrient. A colony with abundant nectar but no pollen will raise little brood; a colony with pollen but no nectar will lack the energy to forage and defend itself. In African contexts, seasonal dearth periods â dry seasons, post-harvest periods, and periods of monoculture flowering â are the critical stress windows where nutrition management determines whether a colony survives or collapses.

2. Natural Forage and Pollen Sources in Africa

African bee forage is highly diverse but seasonally variable. Key nectar and pollen sources vary by agro-ecological zone:

  • Savannah and woodland: Acacia species (Acacia spp.), shea (Vitellaria paradoxa), baobab (Adansonia digitata), marula (Sclerocarya birrea).
  • Forest and highland: Eucalyptus, avocado (Persea americana), coffee (Coffea spp.), macadamia, indigenous forest trees.
  • Farmland and homestead: Sunflower, cowpea, beans, citrus, mango, pawpaw, pumpkin, and many weeds and wildflowers.
  • Coastal and semi-arid: Mangrove, coconut, cashew, sisal, and drought-tolerant shrubs.

For business planning, map your local flowering calendar. A colony needs continuous forage; gaps of even two to three weeks during brood rearing can trigger absconding. Beekeepers who understand their forage calendar can time hive inspections, harvests, and supplemental feeding to match dearth periods.

3. Supplemental Feeding: Sugar Syrup and Pollen Patties

Supplemental feeding is a cost, not a default. Feed only when natural forage is insufficient â during dearth, after harvest, before a pollination contract, or when establishing new colonies. The two main tools are sugar syrup (carbohydrate) and pollen patties (protein).

Table 1: Sugar Syrup Mixing and Feeding Guide (Africa Context)
Purpose Ratio (Sugar : Water) When to Feed Notes for African Beekeepers
Stimulate brood rearing 1 : 1 (thin syrup) Pre-flowering, early build-up Feed small quantities; avoid attracting robbers in dry season
Maintenance during dearth 2 : 1 (thick syrup) Dry season, post-harvest Use internal feeders; reduces robbing and drowning
Emergency rescue 1 : 1 or 2 : 1 When colony is starving Feed at dusk; do not spill syrup near hive entrance
New colony establishment 1 : 1 First 4â6 weeks after transfer Combine with pollen patty if no natural pollen

Source: Adapted from FAO (2009) Beekeeping in Africa, and the Uganda National Apiculture Development Organisation (TUNADO) training materials on colony management.

Pollen patties substitute for natural pollen when it is scarce. A common African recipe uses defatted soy flour, brewer's yeast, sugar, and a small amount of honey or syrup to bind. Commercial pollen substitutes are also available but costlier. For business viability, calculate the cost of feed per hive per dearth month and compare it to the value of the colony and expected honey yield. Feeding is justified when the cost is less than the replacement cost of the colony or the lost pollination income.

Table 2: Pollen Patty Recipe and Feeding Schedule
Ingredient Quantity Function Feeding Frequency
Defatted soy flour 500 g Protein source Place 100â200 g patty on top bars every 7â10 days during dearth. Stop when natural pollen is available.
Brewer's yeast 100 g Vitamins, B-complex
Sugar (granulated) 300 g Energy, binding
Honey or thick syrup 150â200 ml Binding, palatability

Source: Recipe adapted from FAO (2009) Beekeeping in Africa and the International Centre of Insect Physiology and Ecology (ICIPE) beekeeping extension materials for East Africa.

4. Planting for Bees: Bee-Friendly Gardens and Forage Plantations

The most cost-effective long-term nutrition strategy is planting. A bee-friendly garden or forage plot provides continuous nectar and pollen, reduces feed costs, and can generate additional income (fruit, seed, timber, fodder). For African agribusinesses, integrating bee forage into farm boundaries, intercropping, and degraded land restoration creates a dual revenue stream: crop yield from the main enterprise and honey/pollination income from the bees.

Recommended bee-friendly species for African conditions include: sunflower, cowpea, beans, pumpkin, citrus, mango, avocado, cashew, coffee, macadamia, shea, acacia, eucalyptus (use cautiously â invasive in some regions), lavender, basil, and indigenous wildflowers. Avoid planting only one species; diversity ensures staggered flowering and balanced nutrition.

5. Water Sources for Bees

Bees need water for diluting honey, cooling the hive, and raising brood. A colony can consume several litres per week in hot weather. In African dry seasons, water scarcity is a major cause of absconding. Provide a reliable, clean water source within 100â200 metres of the apiary. Use shallow containers with floating sticks or stones so bees do not drown. Keep water shaded to reduce evaporation and algal growth. Never place water sources near pesticide-treated fields or contaminated runoff.

6. Avoiding Pesticide Poisoning

Pesticide poisoning is one of the most destructive and preventable threats to African beekeeping businesses. A single spray event can kill foragers, contaminate honey, and collapse strong colonies. Beekeepers must communicate with farmers, know spray schedules, and protect hives during spraying.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â PESTICIDE POISONING

Never allow bees to forage on crops that have been sprayed with insecticides, especially during flowering. Even "bee-safe" pesticides can kill bees if applied incorrectly. Always:

  • Coordinate with neighbouring farmers before spraying.
  • Close hive entrances with wire mesh or damp cloth during spray days, and provide shade and water inside.
  • Remove honey supers before spraying; do not harvest honey from contaminated hives.
  • Report suspected pesticide kills to local agricultural authorities and keep records for compensation claims.
  • Wash hands, tools, and protective gear after handling pesticides or contaminated equipment.

Quick Reference Checklist â 8 Points for Field Use

  1. Know your forage calendar. Map flowering periods month by month for your area. Identify dearth gaps before they hit.
  2. Inspect colony stores. Check honey and pollen stores every 10â14 days during dearth. A colony with less than 2 kg of stores needs feeding.
  3. Feed the right syrup. Use 1:1 for stimulation, 2:1 for maintenance. Feed at dusk to reduce robbing.
  4. Use pollen patties only when needed. Feed during brood build-up or when natural pollen is absent for more than 7 days.
  5. Plant bee forage. Establish at least 5â10 bee-friendly plant species around your apiary for continuous bloom.
  6. Provide clean water. Keep shallow, shaded water sources with landing sticks within 200 m of hives.
  7. Coordinate with farmers. Know spray schedules. Protect hives during spraying and never harvest contaminated honey.
  8. Record costs and outcomes. Track feed cost per hive, honey yield, and colony survival. Use this data to decide whether feeding or planting is more profitable.

Further Reading â Free Official Resources

  • FAO â Beekeeping in Africa (Agricultural Services Bulletin 68/4) â comprehensive free guide covering forage, feeding, and hive management in African contexts.
  • ICIPE â International Centre of Insect Physiology and Ecology â beekeeping extension materials and research on African bee forage and pollination.
  • Apimondia â International Federation of Beekeepers' Associations â free resources on bee nutrition and sustainable beekeeping.
  • FAO â Pollination and Bee Health â guidance on protecting pollinators from pesticides and maintaining healthy colonies.
  • African Union â Interafrican Bureau for Animal Resources (AU-IBAR) â apiculture development resources for African member states.

Business takeaway: Nutrition and forage management are not optional husbandry tasks â they are the foundation of colony productivity and profitability. Every dollar spent on strategic feeding or forage planting should be justified by increased honey yield, pollination income, or reduced colony losses. Keep records, know your seasons, and treat bee nutrition as an investment, not an expense.

quiz.q: What is the primary carbohydrate source for honey bees?
quiz.explanation: Nectar and honey provide the carbohydrates bees need for energy.

quiz.q: How much honey does a strong colony consume per year?
quiz.explanation: A strong colony consumes 20â30 kg of honey annually for energy.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is essential for brood rearing?
quiz.explanation: Proteins from pollen are critical for brood rearing and gland development.

quiz.q: What is bee bread?
quiz.explanation: Bee bread is pollen packed into cells by bees, used as a protein source.

quiz.q: How much water does a colony use per day in hot weather?
quiz.explanation: A colony uses 1â2 liters of water per day for cooling and dilution.

quiz.q: Which African tree is a key dry-season forage?
quiz.explanation: Acacia species provide nectar and pollen in dry areas of Africa.

quiz.q: How far do bees typically forage from the hive?
quiz.explanation: Bees can forage up to 3 km, but most foraging is within 1 km.

quiz.q: What is a sign of good natural forage?
options: A) Bees returning with pollen loads
quiz.explanation: Pollen loads on bees indicate active foraging and good forage availability.

quiz.q: Which plant flowers in winter and provides critical forage?
quiz.explanation: Aloe species flower in winter, providing forage when little else blooms.

quiz.q: What is the correct sugar-to-water ratio for spring stimulation?
quiz.explanation: A 1:1 ratio (1 kg sugar to 1 liter water) is used for spring stimulation.

quiz.q: Why should you never feed honey from unknown sources?
quiz.explanation: Unknown honey can carry spores of American foulbrood and other diseases.

quiz.q: How often should you feed 1:1 sugar syrup?
quiz.explanation: Feed 500 ml of 1:1 syrup per colony every 3 days.

quiz.q: What is a key ingredient in pollen patties?
quiz.explanation: Soy flour is a common protein source in pollen patties.

quiz.q: Why feed bees at dusk?
quiz.explanation: Feeding at dusk reduces robbing by other bees.

quiz.q: Which plant is fast-growing and flowers in 60â90 days?
quiz.explanation: Sunflower flowers in 60â90 days and provides nectar and pollen.

quiz.q: How many hives can a 10x10 m bee garden support?
quiz.explanation: A small garden with diverse plants can support 1â2 hives.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of planting bee-friendly gardens?
quiz.explanation: Bee gardens provide natural forage, reducing the need for supplemental feeding.

quiz.q: How much water does a colony need daily?
quiz.explanation: A colony uses 1â2 liters of water per day in hot weather.

quiz.q: What is a safe water source for bees?
quiz.explanation: A shallow tray with stones allows bees to land and drink without drowning.

quiz.q: Why add a pinch of salt to bee water?
options: C) To make it taste better
quiz.explanation: Salt provides essential minerals that bees need.

quiz.q: How often should you change bee water?
quiz.explanation: Change water every 2â3 days to prevent mosquito breeding.

quiz.q: What is a sign of pesticide poisoning in bees?
options: A) Dead bees at hive entrance
quiz.explanation: Dead bees at the entrance and disorientation are signs of pesticide poisoning.

quiz.q: When should farmers spray to minimize bee harm?
quiz.explanation: Spraying at dusk when bees are not flying reduces exposure.

quiz.q: Which pesticide is bee-safe?
quiz.explanation: Neem oil is a botanical pesticide that is less toxic to bees.

quiz.q: What should you do if you must spray near hives?
options: A) Cover hives with wet burlap
quiz.explanation: Covering hives with wet burlap reduces pesticide drift into the hive.

quiz.q: How far should hives be from sprayed fields?
quiz.explanation: Keep hives at least 3 km away from sprayed fields to avoid poisoning.

quiz.q: What is integrated pest management (IPM)?
options: B) Combining methods to control pests
quiz.explanation: IPM combines biological, cultural, and chemical methods to manage pests safely.

quiz.q: What is a border crop for bees?
quiz.explanation: Planting sunflower as a border crop can lure bees away from sprayed areas.

quiz.q: What should you do after a pesticide kill?
quiz.explanation: Feeding sugar syrup helps surviving bees recover from pesticide stress.

quiz.q: Why is community education important for pesticide safety?
quiz.explanation: Educating the community promotes bee-friendly practices and reduces poisoning.
